title: How would you estimate how many delivery pizzas the UK orders each week?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many delivery pizzas are ordered in the UK each week?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: The UK orders roughly 7 million delivery pizzas a week: about 4.2M orders (15% of 28M households ordering in a typical week) at 1.7 pizzas each. Keep orders and pizzas apart from the start, because a delivery platform is paid per order and a pizza maker per pizza. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many delivery pizzas are ordered in the UK each week?

Set the boundaries first:

  • Delivery only: pizzas brought to the door by the restaurant or a delivery app. Collection, dine-in and frozen supermarket pizzas are out.
  • Homes, not offices: office lunch orders exist, but they are small next to evening household orders. Mention them and leave them out.
  • Unit: pizzas, as asked, but work out orders on the way.
"I'll estimate pizzas delivered to UK homes in a typical week, going via the number of orders, and exclude collection and frozen pizza."

The approach: households × weekly ordering rate × pizzas per order

A pizza order is a household decision: one family, one order, several pizzas. So start from households, not people. A weekly question also changes how you think about frequency: instead of "how many times a year", ask "what share of homes order in a given week?"

Households × share ordering this week × pizzas per order.

Step by step

  1. UK households: 28M (the ONS counted about 28.6M in 2024).
  2. Share ordering in a typical week: 15%. Build it rather than guess it: assume 60% of households order delivery pizza at least sometimes, and those households order about once every four weeks. 60% × ¼ = 15%.
  3. Orders a week: 28M × 15% = 4.2M orders.
  4. Pizzas per order: 1.7. A single person orders one, a couple often two, a family two or three. 1.7 is a fair average.
  5. Pizzas a week: 4.2M × 1.7 = about 7.1M pizzas.

That is about 1M delivery pizzas a day on average, with far more on Friday and Saturday nights.

Sanity check from a second angle

From the supply side. Assume about 15,000 outlets deliver pizza in the UK, from chains to independent takeaways, and each handles about 280 delivery orders a week (40 a night). 15,000 × 280 = 4.2M orders, matching the demand side. Both inputs are assumptions, but two independent routes landing in the same place is reassuring.

Against the market leader. Domino's Pizza Group reported system sales of about $2.1B for 2025 across about 1,400 UK and Irish stores (converted from pounds at roughly $1.30). At an assumed $30 per order, that is about 69M orders a year, or 1.3M a week, covering both delivery and collection. If two thirds are deliveries, Domino's delivers about 0.9M orders a week, roughly a fifth of our 4.2M. The largest chain holding about a fifth of a fragmented market, alongside Pizza Hut, Papa John's and thousands of independents, is plausible.

Which assumption matters most?

The weekly ordering share. At 10% instead of 15%, orders fall to 2.8M and pizzas to about 4.8M a week. Pizzas per order matters less: it moves pizzas but not orders.

What a strong answer sounds like

"About 7 million pizzas a week from 4.2 million orders. I got the 15% weekly ordering rate from 60% of homes ordering about once a month. A supply-side check, 15,000 outlets at about 280 orders a week, gives the same 4.2 million orders. If you're a delivery app, the 4.2 million orders is your number, and Friday and Saturday will carry a big share of it."

A weak answer multiplies 68M people by "maybe one pizza a month" and divides by four, mixing people, orders and pizzas in one step so nobody can follow or test it.

Common mistakes

  • Treating orders and pizzas as one unit. 7.1M pizzas is not 7.1M orders. Platforms earn per order.
  • Starting from people. Pizza is ordered for the household, so you would overcount.
  • Using the weekly average for staffing. Demand is concentrated on weekend evenings, so a restaurant staffed for the average is short-handed when it matters.
  • Stopping at gross sales. For a restaurant case, what matters is contribution per order after ingredients, packaging, labour and delivery commission.

Practise it

1. Friday and Saturday together take 40% of weekly orders. How many orders is that per weekend night, compared with an average night?

Show the answer

40% × 4.2M = 1.68M orders over two nights, so 840,000 a night. The average night is 4.2M ÷ 7 = 600,000. Weekend nights run 40% above average.

2. At $30 per order, how much do UK households spend on delivered pizza a year?

Show the answer

4.2M orders × $30 = $126M a week × 52 = about $6.6B a year.

3. A delivery app handles all these orders and charges restaurants a 30% commission. What would its commission revenue be, and why is that number an overstatement?

Show the answer

$6.55B × 30% = about $2.0B a year. It overstates the app's opportunity because chains like Domino's mostly run their own delivery, and many independents use their own drivers. The app's real market is the share of orders placed through it.

Where to practise next

For another household-based estimate, try parcels delivered to UK homes. To go beyond the sizing into the business, read how restaurants and fast-food chains make money and how platforms work. Timed practice is in the market sizing drills.
